source: Ruggeri et al. (2020) Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk
finding: Large preregistered replication of the 1979 and 1981 prospect theory problems. The empirical base replicates well, with some shrinkage.
numbers: N=4,098, 19 countries, 13 languages. 94% of items replicated (attenuated). 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated. Some countries reached 100%.
quote: empirical foundations of prospect theory replicate
limits: Only the abstract page was readable; the body is paywalled, so effect sizes per item and the one failed contrast are not recorded. Original method used hypothetical stakes. Heterogeneity between countries and within persons.
agent_relevance: Framing and the certainty effect are stable human patterns, so a model trained on human text can inherit them. It does not say we should copy them.

source: Territorial prospect theory replication (OSF preprint v2, replicating Ruggeri et al.)
finding: Two preregistered replications with territorial instead of financial dilemmas. Certainty, framing, isolation and small-probability overweighting held. Reflection did not.
numbers: US N=149, UK N=253. Item-level replication 69% (US) and 81% (UK). Theoretical contrasts replicated 77% and 92%.
limits: Abstract only. Small samples. Reflection effect (risk seeking over losses) failed outside money.
agent_relevance: Reflection is the weakest leg of the theory. Do not code risk seeking after a loss into an agent as a law.

source: Walasek and Stewart (2015) How to make loss aversion disappear and reverse
finding: Loss aversion depends on the range of gains and losses in the lottery set (decision by sampling). Equal ranges give none; a wider loss range reverses it.
quote: we find no loss aversion at all when we use symmetric ranges
limits: Exp 2 reversed condition gave 1.01, not below 1. Exp 3 small. Mostly MTurk with hypothetical stakes. The real-world asymmetric-experience account is proposed, not tested.
agent_relevance: Loss aversion is a property of the option set, not a fixed trait. A fair test of a model needs symmetric and asymmetric ranges.

source: Yechiam (2019) Acceptable losses: the debatable origins of loss aversion
finding: Review of early gain and loss utility studies. Only very large losses are overweighted; smaller losses often are not. Some studies were cited as support when they found no loss aversion.
numbers: No new numbers. Abstract summary only.
limits: Read through the Europe PMC abstract only. Review by a leading critic.
agent_relevance: Loss aversion may be limited to large stakes. Test small and large stakes separately.

source: Gal and Rucker (2018) The Loss of Loss Aversion (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Critique that status quo bias, endowment and safe-option preference are better explained by inertia and loss attention than by a loss weight. Reply articles exist.
numbers: Gal (2006) inertia account; Gal and Rucker J Consum Psychol 28(3):497-516. No numbers in the source.
limits: Secondary source. The primary paper (403 error) was not opened.
agent_relevance: Rival explanations (inertia, attention) predict different manipulations. Check them before trusting a loss-weight story.

source: Yechiam and Hochman (2013) Losses as modulators of attention (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Rival to loss aversion: losses raise attention and arousal, with an inverse U effect on performance, without a heavier subjective weight.
numbers: Cited evidence: golf putting (Pope and Schweitzer 2011), arousal (Hochman and Yechiam 2011), hot stove effect. No numbers in the source.
limits: Secondary source. Loss attention can also debias.
agent_relevance: A loss framing may mainly raise effort and care rather than bias choice. Worth a cheap test.

source: Mrkva, Johnson, Gaechter, Herrmann (2020) Moderating Loss Aversion (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Loss aversion replicated in five samples and its size varies in predictable ways with moderators.
numbers: Five unique samples. No coefficients in the source.
limits: Secondary source only; primary not opened.
agent_relevance: Loss aversion is context-dependent but real in many designs.

source: Brown, Imai, Vieider, Camerer (2024) Meta-analysis of empirical estimates of loss aversion (via Tarabeih 2026)
finding: Broadest human meta-analysis. Pooled loss aversion about 1.96, supporting the strong claim.
numbers: lambda=1.96, 95% CI 1.82 to 2.11. About 150 studies, eclectic inclusion.
limits: Not opened (publisher 403). Numbers come from a 2026 meta-analysis that cites it. Includes ordered designs with losses smaller than gains.
agent_relevance: Upper anchor for human loss aversion.

source: Walasek, Mullett, Stewart (2024) meta-analysis of loss aversion (via Tarabeih 2026)
finding: A meta-analysis on a smaller set of studies with complete data gives a middle estimate.
numbers: lambda=1.31.
limits: Not opened. Value taken from Tarabeih 2026.
agent_relevance: Middle anchor. Meta-analytic loss aversion depends on which studies are included.

source: Yechiam and Zeif (2025) Loss aversion is not robust: a re-meta-analysis (via Tarabeih 2026)
finding: Re-analysis finds the human coefficient depends on design: about 2.3 when losses are smaller than gains (ordered), about 1.07 when gains and losses are symmetric.
numbers: lambda=1.07 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.18) for symmetric unordered designs; about 2.3 for ordered designs with losses smaller than gains.
limits: Not opened. Numbers via Tarabeih 2026. Authors are known critics.
agent_relevance: Loss aversion may partly be a design artefact. An agent should not assume 2.25.

source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect Theory in Large Language Models: a meta-analysis
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis of every fitted prospect theory parameter in LLM choice studies. LLMs show modest loss aversion, near-linear value in one fit method, and human-like probability weighting.
numbers: 102 estimates, 11 studies, 32 models. Pooled lambda 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46; 28 estimates); prediction interval 0.20 to 2.31. Symmetric designs: 1.15 vs human 1.07. Losses smaller than gains: 1.46 vs human 2.3. Curvature 1.01 (Tversky-Kahneman fit) vs human 0.67; 0.52 (Tanaka fit) vs 0.67. Probability weighting 0.81 and 0.84.
limits: Preprint. Few studies for weighting. Some standard errors imputed. Estimates from the same study are dependent.
agent_relevance: Best single summary. LLM loss aversion is weak and model-specific, so measure the model you use.

source: Tarabeih (2026) moderators of LLM loss aversion
finding: Model family and release year explain much of the spread in LLM loss aversion. Persona prompts and gain-loss structure did not.
numbers: Family R2=.27 (F(4,23)=3.29, p=.029). Gemini +0.69 vs GPT (p=.021). Small open models -0.49 (p=.063). Release year -0.16 per year (p=.032), R2=.38. Stakes +0.35 per tenfold increase (p=.030). GPT-3.5 lambda 2.72, GPT-4.1 0.57.
limits: Year decline rests mainly on one GPT lineage and lost significance in some robustness checks. Designs are confounded with models.
agent_relevance: Newer, better-aligned models drift towards loss neutrality. Bias is not a fixed cost of using an LLM.

source: Jia et al. (2024) Decision-making behavior evaluation framework for LLMs under uncertain context
finding: Fits risk, probability weighting and loss aversion for three commercial LLMs on multiple-price-list lotteries. Estimates differ a lot by model.
numbers: 300 responses per model. Context-free lambda: GPT-4-Turbo 1.48, Claude-3-Opus 6.32, Gemini-1.0-Pro 2.33; human sample 3.47. Risk (sigma) 0.60, 0.31, 0.50 vs human 0.48. With random persona demographics Claude lambda fell to 2.60; real-world distributions 2.17.
limits: Financial lotteries only. Repeated queries in one session may not be independent. Persona effects are a proxy.
agent_relevance: The same prompt gave loss aversion from 1.5 to 6.3 depending on model. Persona framing alone moved Claude's lambda by more than half.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Rethinking prospect theory for LLMs
finding: Prospect theory fits many LLMs poorly. Bigger models fit better, but loss aversion stays unstable, and verbal probabilities break the fit.
limits: Models told not to compute expected value. Some lambda values sit on fit boundaries (0.010, 4.000).
agent_relevance: Check fit before reading a parameter. Boundary values mean no stable reference-dependent preference.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping behavioral biases via utility theory
finding: LLMs are neither human-like nor rational. Weaker loss aversion, similar risk aversion, stronger time discounting. Prompting to change bias works inconsistently.
numbers: 56 game settings; N=100 samples at temperature 1 (GPT-4 prompt tests N=10). Direct prompting and zero-shot chain of thought gave no reliable shift. One-shot example shifted risk and loss aversion. Two-shot confounded gain and loss examples. Role-playing teenager or senior lowered loss aversion.
limits: Models may recall the games from training. Role-play differs from advice mode.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to be less loss averse does not work; showing one worked example did. The scaffold should use examples, not instructions.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 replicated three of six Kahneman and Tversky biases: framing, certainty effect, and overweighting of small probability differences.
numbers: 3 of 6 biases replicated. Small changes to vignette wording derailed answers.
limits: Old model. Full text read for this section.
agent_relevance: Surface wording changes can flip answers, so a bias seen in one prompt may not generalise.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The Emergence of Economic Rationality of GPT
finding: GPT choices are more consistent with utility maximisation than human choices, but fragile to a change in framing.
numbers: Mean CCEI 0.998 (risk), 0.997, 0.997, 0.999 vs human 0.980, 0.985, 0.967, 0.963. Price framing cut risk CCEI to 0.901 (34% below 0.9); time 0.884, social 0.698, food 0.894.
limits: Budget-allocation tasks, not lotteries.
agent_relevance: Rationality in one frame does not carry over. Test several frames.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 showed a framing effect like humans in a medicine efficacy task.
numbers: Positive frame rated 5 (11 of 11 trials); negative frame rated 4 (11 of 11). Humans 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Single task, near-deterministic output.
agent_relevance: Framing sensitivity is real and cheap to trigger.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Framework of 13,465 prompts for bias, with a self-help debiasing method where the model rewrites its own prompt.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. Self-help method reduced biased answers (abstract gives no effect size).
limits: Abstract only; no numbers.
agent_relevance: A debiasing step that rewrites the prompt is a candidate operator.

source: Yechiam and Tarabeih (2026) Mimicry without understanding
finding: LLM loss aversion depends on what the prompt says about human loss aversion. A stronger reported bias in the paper gives a stronger model bias.
numbers: ChatGPT-4o lambda 1.09 with no paper; 1.79 after the Brown et al. abstract; 1.52 after the full report. Qwen showed the same direction.
limits: Authors are loss aversion critics. Two models only.
agent_relevance: Mentioning a bias in the prompt can switch it on. Do not describe biases to the model unless needed.

source: Marks and Vollberg (2026) The psychophysics of affect in LLMs
finding: When asked how outcomes would feel, models rated gains more strongly than equal losses (reverse of loss aversion). In choice, the asymmetry mostly disappeared.
numbers: Gain scale above loss scale in 8 of 9 models (+1.2 to +24.3, p<.001). Choice lambda 0.88 to 1.59; kimi-k2.5 1.07-1.28, gpt-5-nano 1.005-1.04, vs human 2.25 and 1.96. Rating asymmetry shrank when outcomes were shown together.
limits: Simulated participants (30 per model). Affect ratings are text, not feelings.
agent_relevance: Stated feelings and choices disagree in a model. Do not use a model's self-report of how a loss feels as an input.

source: Yee and Koh (2026) LLMs as calibrated measurement instruments for behavioral parameters
finding: Default LLM agents show attenuated loss aversion. Profile prompts push it to or past human values.
numbers: 4 models, 24,000 agent-scenario pairs. Baseline lambda 1.18 (GPT-4o), 1.12 (4o-mini), 1.90 (Gemini 2.5 Pro), 1.46 (Claude 3.5 Haiku). Biased profile max 3.00 (d=1.82, p<.001). Human benchmark 2.25. Gamble vs disposition correlation 0.42.
limits: Preprint from a small lab. Calibration range is set by the authors' prompts.
agent_relevance: Profile prompts steer risk behaviour in either direction, so any persona in a scaffold changes it.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Developmental trajectories of decision making in LLMs
finding: Across successive OpenAI models, risk taking rose but loss aversion fell below neutral and choices became more deterministic.
numbers: Lambda fell below 1 in newer models (abstract; exact values not extracted).
limits: Gambling task with happiness ratings; one vendor.
agent_relevance: Fits the meta-analytic decline with release year.

source: AI decision under risk with framing (GPT-4o, o3, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 1.5 Pro; arXiv 2508.00902)
finding: Loss-frame minus gain-frame risk scores were positive in about 71% of model-scenario pairs, but the sign reversed in some scenarios. Math scenarios showed no framing.
numbers: 25 of 35 pairs positive (my count). Championship scenario +1.40 to +1.84; Career Transition negative for all models (-0.37 to -0.60). Math: o3 and GPT-4o chose the sure option 399 of 399 trials. 25 runs per cell.
limits: Internal count errors in the paper and no human baseline. No lambda estimated.
agent_relevance: Framing effects depend on scenario content. Where the task has a clear expected value, they vanish.

source: GPT-4.1 persona betting study (arXiv 2603.15831)
finding: GPT-4.1 given wealth personas bet very differently, read by the author as reference-point effects. Not a direct test.
numbers: 6,950 decisions. Mean rounds: rich 1.11, middle 7.83, poor 37.39 (H=393.5). Risk score 17.5, 40.2, 63.4; poor vs rich d=4.15.
limits: No gain/loss test and no lambda. Wealth is confounded with stake scale (200x).
agent_relevance: A persona's stated situation changes risk-taking a lot. Keep the scaffold's framing neutral.

source: Human curvature and weighting benchmarks (Tversky and Kahneman 1992; Tanaka et al. 2010; Imai et al. 2025; via Tarabeih 2026)
finding: Reference values for diminishing sensitivity and probability weighting in people.
numbers: Curvature 0.67, weighting 0.68 (Imai et al., CI 0.66 to 0.70); Tversky and Kahneman 0.88 and 0.65; Tanaka 0.67 and 0.685.
limits: Not opened. Via Tarabeih 2026.
agent_relevance: Probability weighting is the best-supported human regularity and the one LLMs keep.

source: Tarabeih (2026) publication bias and reasoning-model check
finding: No sign of funnel asymmetry in LLM loss aversion estimates, but too few studies to rule bias out. Reasoning models did not weight probabilities differently.
numbers: Egger p=.58, Begg p=.37, k=10 studies. Three reasoning models share weighting 0.81. No release-year trend in weighting.
limits: Tanaka pools rest on two studies and exclusion of two extreme fits.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode alone does not remove probability distortion.

source: Description-experience gap and LLM studies (via Tarabeih 2026)
finding: Humans overweight rare events when told probabilities and underweight them when learned by sampling. Almost all LLM work uses described gambles.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Second-hand on the human gap (Hertwig et al. 2004).
agent_relevance: A scaffold that samples outcomes may behave differently from one that reads stated odds.
